paragraphs: LLM agents often spend substantial time and money planning how to complete a task. Reusing a previous answer is insufficient when the answer depends on changing external information or environmental conditions. Agentic Plan Caching instead reuses the structure of a successful workflow, allowing the agent to carry useful planning experience into related requests.

The system extracts structured plan templates from completed agent executions and stores them during use. For a new request, keyword extraction helps identify relevant cached plans. Lightweight models then adapt a selected template to the specific task and its context. This makes the stored memory a reusable starting point for planning, while still allowing the resulting plan to reflect current circumstances.

Across the evaluated real-world agent applications, the approach reduced costs by an average of 50.31% and latency by 27.28% while maintaining performance. These findings show that reusing planning structure can reduce repeated reasoning work. The framework also complements existing infrastructure for serving language models, making plan reuse an additional source of efficiency.
neurips-2025-agentic-plan-caching-test-t.tldr: Agentic Plan Caching reuses and adapts successful workflow templates to reduce agent costs and latency while maintaining performance in the reported evaluations.

paragraphs: Skeleton-based zero-shot action recognition asks a model to identify previously unseen action classes from skeletal representations. Skeleton-Cache addresses the challenge of improving these predictions during inference, without further training or access to the original training data. Its central idea is to make recognition a lightweight retrieval process over stored representations.

The cache combines descriptors that capture the skeleton globally with descriptors that preserve finer local information. These views can contribute differently to recognizing different actions. To combine their predictions, the framework uses a language model's semantic reasoning to assign importance weights for each action class. The resulting prediction therefore draws on both structured skeleton information and class-specific guidance about which descriptors matter.

Experiments on NTU RGB+D 60/120 and PKU-MMD II show consistent improvements across several recognition backbones. The gains occur in both zero-shot and generalized zero-shot settings. The findings support using an external cache and semantic weighting as a way to adapt existing recognizers to unseen actions without introducing another training stage.
neurips-2025-boosting-skeleton-based-zer.tldr: Skeleton-Cache improves recognition of unseen actions through retrieval over skeleton descriptors weighted by language-model semantic guidance.

paragraphs: Video temporal grounding locates the portion of a video that matches a written query. The paper addresses two problems: models may rely on superficial associations learned from biased datasets, and they often assume the requested event must appear somewhere. Together, these behaviors can produce confident matches that do not reflect the video's actual content.

CausalVTG combines three mechanisms. A causality-aware encoder uses front-door adjustment to reduce confounding in visual and textual information. A temporal module reconstructs query-conditioned video features at multiple resolutions, helping represent events at different time scales. A counterfactual contrastive objective additionally trains the model to distinguish genuinely relevant queries from those that are not grounded in the video.

Across five benchmarks, the framework outperforms the compared state-of-the-art methods. It achieves more precise localization under stricter overlap requirements and better identifies whether a query has a valid match at all. The results support treating relevance detection and precise temporal localization as connected problems, with causal reasoning helping address both.
neurips-2025-causalvtg-towards-robust-vi.tldr: CausalVTG combines causal feature learning, multiscale temporal modeling, and counterfactual training to improve segment localization and detect absent queried events.

paragraphs: The paper studies whether reinforcement learning becomes computationally manageable when value functions have a linear representation. Its setting, partial policy-value realizability, assumes this representation exists for every policy in a specified set. The goal is to learn a policy within epsilon of the best performance in that set. This assumption lies between requiring linear representations for all policy values and requiring one only for the optimal value.

The authors prove hardness for two important policy sets. For parameterized greedy policies, they establish NP-hardness. For sets containing softmax policies, they give a lower bound exponential in feature dimension under the Randomized Exponential Time Hypothesis, with the stated qualification unless NP equals RP. Their proofs reduce variants of Max-3SAT to the corresponding reinforcement learning problems.

These results show that extending realizability beyond the optimal policy does not, by itself, remove computational barriers in the studied settings. The contrast with positive results under full policy-value realizability and generative access clarifies why the exact scope of a representation assumption matters for algorithmic guarantees.
neurips-2025-computational-hardness-of-r.tldr: Partial linear realizability of policy values still permits computationally hard reinforcement learning problems under the paper's studied policy classes and complexity assumptions.

paragraphs: Brain atlases group neuroimaging measurements into regions, reducing data complexity and supporting interpretation. Many existing atlases use fixed templates shared across people, which limits flexibility in both regional detail and individual organization. Deep Cluster Atlas addresses this by generating individualized brain partitions at the voxel level, with control over resolution and the anatomical area being analyzed.

DCA combines a pretrained autoencoder with graph-guided deep clustering and spatial regularization. The learned representation supports grouping by functional characteristics, while the spatial component encourages regions to remain contiguous. This combination targets regions whose measurements are functionally coherent and whose locations form connected areas. The framework can also be applied to different brain structures.

The authors introduce a standardized evaluation platform using multiple large fMRI datasets. Across the tested datasets and scales, DCA improves functional homogeneity by 98.8% and silhouette coefficient by 29% over state-of-the-art atlases. It also improves the evaluated autism diagnosis and cognitive decoding tasks. Fine-tuning the pretrained model further improves results for the corresponding task.
neurips-2025-dca-graph-guided-deep-embed.tldr: DCA learns individualized, spatially contiguous brain regions and improves atlas quality and downstream performance in the reported fMRI evaluations.

paragraphs: Detecting anomalies in a time series requires understanding how measurements evolve and identifying where unusual behavior occurs. The paper investigates why language models have struggled with this task, sometimes trailing simple methods. Its analysis identifies two central difficulties: interpreting complex temporal dynamics and accurately locating anomalies within the sequence.

The proposed method combines statistical decomposition with index-aware prompting. Decomposition separates aspects of the time series to make its structure easier to analyze, while index-aware prompts explicitly address positions in the sequence. The pairing targets both identified weaknesses: understanding the pattern and connecting an anomaly judgment to the appropriate location.

On AnomLLM, the method outperforms 21 existing prompting strategies, with F1 improvements reaching 66.6%. A separate comparison against 16 non-language-model baselines on TSB-AD identifies situations where contextual reasoning gives language models distinctive advantages. The findings therefore concern both how to improve these models and when their reasoning capabilities can be useful; they do not establish that language models dominate every anomaly-detection setting.
neurips-2025-delving-into-large-language.tldr: Statistical decomposition and index-aware prompting address language models' temporal understanding and localization weaknesses, improving anomaly detection in the reported benchmarks.

paragraphs: Mixture-of-experts models save computation by activating only some experts for each input, but storing every expert still consumes substantial memory. This paper studies whether a model specialized for one domain needs its entire expert collection. The authors observe that a few demonstrations from that domain lead to a sparse, stable subset of experts being activated on related tasks.

EASY-EP uses this behavior to identify experts worth retaining. Its importance assessment considers both routing scores and the size of activated experts' outputs, so routing preference is only part of the judgment. It also estimates token contributions using similarities between representations before and after routed experts. These two components guide pruning toward experts that contribute to the demonstrated domain.

Experiments on DeepSeek-R1 and DeepSeek-V3-0324 show comparable performance with half the experts and 2.99 times the throughput under the same memory budget as the full model. The result supports domain-specific pruning as a way to convert sparse usage into memory savings, using only a few demonstrations to guide specialization.
neurips-2025-domain-specific-pruning-of-.tldr: EASY-EP uses a few domain examples to retain relevant experts, achieving comparable tested performance with half the experts and higher throughput.

paragraphs: Turbulence is difficult to simulate because motion at different scales interacts. Direct numerical simulation resolves this behavior in detail, but its computational demands motivate learned alternatives. EddyFormer combines a Transformer with a spectral-element architecture to model large three-dimensional turbulent flows while retaining information about both local and broader flow structure.

Its tokenization separates the flow into grid-scale and subgrid-scale components. This gives the model a representation designed around the multiple scales involved in turbulence. The architecture pairs spectral methods' accuracy with attention's scalability. The authors also create a three-dimensional isotropic turbulence dataset for training and evaluating the approach.

On that task, EddyFormer achieves reported DNS-level accuracy at 256 cubed resolution with a 30-fold speedup. In unseen domains up to four times larger than those used for training, it preserves accuracy on energy spectra, correlation functions, and structure functions. On The Well benchmark, it reproduces complex dynamics in cases where previous machine-learning models fail to converge, supporting its usefulness across the evaluated flow conditions.
neurips-2025-eddyformer-accelerated-neur.tldr: EddyFormer combines spectral-element representations with attention to accelerate three-dimensional turbulence simulation and generalize to larger tested domains.

paragraphs: Inductive reasoning means inferring a hidden rule from a limited set of examples. This paper tests the assumption that generating a chain of reasoning improves that ability. The authors build four controlled tasks based on chess, Texas Hold'em, dice games, and blackjack, each governed by hidden rules defined by humans.

In these tasks, chain-of-thought reasoning can reduce accuracy, and reasoning models often perform worse than their non-reasoning counterparts. The proposed theoretical explanation identifies three places where errors can accumulate: dividing a problem into the wrong subtasks, solving those subtasks incorrectly, and incorrectly combining intermediate results into a final answer. Extra reasoning steps can therefore create additional opportunities for error amplification.

The authors use these failure categories to design interventions that structure chain-of-thought generation. These improve inductive accuracy without retraining the models. The findings suggest that the organization and reliability of intermediate steps matter alongside their number. They challenge the expectation that more explicit reasoning will automatically improve the discovery of unfamiliar rules.
neurips-2025-evaluating-the-inductive-ab.tldr: Controlled game tasks show that chain-of-thought can hurt hidden-rule inference, while interventions targeting specific reasoning failures improve accuracy without retraining.

paragraphs: Data assimilation combines observations with a dynamical model to estimate a system's state. The paper highlights a tension between methods that assume the true dynamics are known and deterministic learned mappings that miss stochastic behavior. It also identifies shortcomings in diffusion approaches that generate a state in one shot without maintaining physical consistency across successive transitions.

FlowDAS learns state transitions using stochastic interpolants, producing a sequence of updates that includes randomness. Observations enter each transition, so measurement information guides the evolving prediction throughout the process. This stepwise design connects the representation of stochastic dynamics with repeated adjustment to the available evidence, enabling stable forecasts consistent with measurements.

The experiments cover Lorenz-63, Navier–Stokes tasks involving super-resolution or sparse observations, and large-scale weather forecasting. In these settings, the underlying dynamics are partly or entirely unknown. FlowDAS outperforms the tested model-driven approaches, neural operators, and score-based methods in accuracy and physical plausibility. The results support learning observation-guided stochastic transitions for assimilation when complete dynamical knowledge is unavailable.
neurips-2025-flowdas-a-stochastic-interp.tldr: FlowDAS learns stepwise stochastic state transitions guided by observations, improving data assimilation in tested systems with incompletely known dynamics.

paragraphs: Force prompting lets users control generated video through physical signals, such as a push at one location or a wind field across a scene. The paper investigates whether pretrained video models can turn these controls into realistic motion. A central obstacle is collecting paired forces and videos: real forces are difficult to measure, while simulated videos have limited appearance quality and diversity.

The authors adapt a pretrained model using Blender-generated examples involving a limited collection of objects. The model then generalizes force-conditioned generation across varied geometries, environments, and materials. At inference, it uses the physical prior learned by the video model without requiring a physics simulator or a three-dimensional asset.

Training uses around 15,000 examples and one day on four A100 GPUs. The approach outperforms the compared methods on force adherence and physical realism. Ablations identify visual diversity and specific training text keywords as important to generalization. These findings suggest that limited simulated demonstrations can help expose useful physical control capabilities in pretrained video models.
neurips-2025-force-prompting-video-gener.tldr: Force prompting adapts pretrained video models with simulated examples so generated scenes respond to physical controls without a simulator at inference.

paragraphs: Graph foundation models need substantial graph data, including meaningful text attached to nodes. Traditional synthesis methods emphasize simple structural changes and struggle to supply this semantic content. Directly asking a language model to generate graphs introduces other difficulties, including limited context, hallucinated content, and inconsistent relationships between the generated text and graph structure.

GraphMaster organizes synthesis around four specialized language-model agents: Manager, Perception, Enhancement, and Evaluation. They collaborate through repeated refinement to improve semantic coherence and structural integrity. The framework treats graph generation as a coordinated process in which the content and organization of the graph are developed together.

The authors create data-limited versions of six standard graph benchmarks to evaluate this setting. They also assess interpretability using human judgments and a mathematical analysis based on Grassmannian manifolds, providing qualitative and quantitative views of semantic coherence. GraphMaster significantly outperforms traditional synthesis approaches across multiple datasets. The results support coordinated agent-based synthesis as a way to improve graph data availability when source examples are scarce.
neurips-2025-graphmaster-automated-graph.tldr: GraphMaster coordinates four language-model agents to synthesize semantically coherent, structurally consistent graph data from limited examples.

paragraphs: Vision-language-action models transfer knowledge from pretrained vision-language models into control policies for physical systems. This creates a practical mismatch: powerful pretrained models can be too large for real-time control, and their discrete token outputs differ from the continuous commands robots require. Specialized action modules address these control requirements by adding new parameters to the pretrained system.

The paper examines what happens when those modules are continuous action experts based on diffusion or flow matching. The authors find that simply attaching such experts can substantially slow training and harm knowledge transfer. This makes the interaction between the new control module and the existing backbone an important part of the learning problem.

Through an extensive analysis of design choices, the authors study their effects on performance and preservation of semantic knowledge. They propose a technique that insulates the vision-language backbone during action-model training, mitigating the observed problems. The contribution is a way to improve how pretrained understanding and newly learned control are combined, addressing training dynamics as well as the demands of robot action generation.
neurips-2025-knowledge-insulating-vision.tldr: Insulating a pretrained vision-language backbone mitigates the training slowdown and impaired knowledge transfer caused by naively adding continuous action experts.

paragraphs: A model's response to conflicting information reveals only part of what it knows. KScope instead characterizes knowledge using both correctness and consistency, distinguishing five possible statuses. This provides a richer description of a model's relationship to a question than simply checking whether its stored knowledge disagrees with supplied context.

The framework uses a hierarchy of statistical tests to refine hypotheses about the model's knowledge modes and assign a status. Applied to nine language models across four datasets, it shows that supporting context narrows knowledge gaps. Context difficulty, relevance, and familiarity are associated with successful updates, making the properties of the supplied information central to understanding when it helps.

The study also finds that models have similar preferences for context features when partially correct or conflicted, but differ sharply when consistently wrong. Guided by this feature analysis, context summarization combined with increased credibility improves update effectiveness and generalizes across models. KScope therefore connects measurement of existing knowledge with evidence about how to present useful new information.
neurips-2025-kscope-a-framework-for-char.tldr: KScope statistically classifies five language-model knowledge statuses and identifies context properties that improve knowledge updates across evaluated models.

paragraphs: Tissue development involves coordinated changes among neighboring cells, including changes in their states and spatial arrangement. Spatial transcriptomics captures tissue organization across space and time, but methods focused on individual cells can overlook this neighborhood-level evolution. NicheFlow models cellular microenvironments to capture the joint development of nearby cells.

The framework represents each local neighborhood as a point cloud and infers its trajectory across sequential spatial slides. It uses optimal transport and Variational Flow Matching to jointly model changes in cell states and spatial coordinates. Keeping those quantities together allows the inferred trajectory to describe both how a neighborhood's cellular composition changes and how its spatial organization evolves.

Across diverse spatiotemporal datasets covering embryonic and brain development, NicheFlow recovers global spatial architecture and local microenvironment composition. These findings support analyzing tissue evolution at a scale that links individual cell states to their surrounding organization. The resulting trajectories provide a model of coordinated neighborhood change inferred from sequential observations of tissue.
neurips-2025-modeling-microenvironment-t.tldr: NicheFlow infers how cellular neighborhoods evolve by jointly modeling cell states and spatial positions across sequential tissue observations.

paragraphs: Low-rank inverse approximations make matrix computations more scalable, but the matrices used in practice may contain noise from sampling, sketching, or quantization. This paper studies how much that noise changes a rank-limited inverse approximation. It measures the change in spectral norm for symmetric matrices, focusing on the largest directional error.

Under mild noise assumptions, the authors derive sharp bounds that apply at finite matrix sizes. The bounds connect error to eigenvalue separation, spectral decay, and how noise aligns with low-curvature directions. Their mathematical approach applies contour integration to the reciprocal function, whose singularity makes it different from functions that are well-behaved everywhere.

The resulting bounds improve on naive adaptations of classical full-inverse bounds by as much as a factor of the square root of matrix dimension. In experiments with synthetic and real-world matrices, they closely follow observed perturbation errors, while classical estimates often substantially overpredict them. The contribution is a more informative, spectrum-sensitive account of robustness for low-rank inverse calculations in noisy settings.
neurips-2025-perturbation-bounds-for-low.tldr: New spectrum-aware perturbation bounds more tightly characterize how noise affects low-rank inverse approximations under the paper's assumptions.

paragraphs: Classifying nodes in graphs with textual attributes presents complementary challenges for graph neural networks and language models. Graph networks process connected data efficiently but depend heavily on labeled examples. Language models can work with few or no labels, yet applying them at scale is difficult. Different local graph structures also make it hard for one graph-learning mechanism to suit every node.

The proposed preference-driven distillation framework transfers knowledge in two stages. First, a selector guided by graph-network preferences chooses nodes to support transfer of language-model predictions into teacher graph networks. Then a second selector uses node preferences to identify the most suitable teacher for each node. Those selected teachers provide tailored supervision to a student graph network.

Experiments on real-world text-attributed graphs validate the framework for few-shot node classification. The approach matters because it accounts for variation on both sides of knowledge transfer: which nodes help particular teachers learn, and which teacher best suits a particular node. This brings language-model knowledge and multiple graph-learning approaches into one student.
neurips-2025-preference-driven-knowledge.tldr: Preference-driven distillation transfers language-model knowledge through multiple graph teachers, selecting suitable supervision for each node before training a student.

paragraphs: Articulated objects require three-dimensional representations that capture both detailed surfaces and changes in configuration. REArtGS addresses these goals together using multi-view RGB images of an object in two states. It augments a representation built from three-dimensional Gaussian primitives with constraints on geometry and motion, supporting reconstruction of observed states and generation of unseen ones.

For surface reconstruction, the method uses unbiased signed distance field guidance to regularize Gaussian opacity fields. This supplies geometric guidance intended to improve the recovered surface. For movement, it learns deformation fields constrained by the object's kinematic structure. Those constraints connect changes in the Gaussian representation to the object's articulated motion, enabling unsupervised generation of surface meshes in new states.

Experiments on synthetic and real datasets demonstrate high-quality textured reconstructions of the supplied states and high-fidelity surfaces for unseen states. The findings support combining surface-oriented geometric guidance with motion constraints, so a single framework can recover appearance and shape while also representing how the articulated object changes configuration.
neurips-2025-reartgs-reconstructing-and-.tldr: REArtGS combines geometric and kinematic constraints on 3D Gaussians to reconstruct articulated objects and generate surfaces in unseen configurations.

paragraphs: Learning a new task from examples requires finding a rule that carries beyond those examples. Program synthesis provides a structured way to search for such rules, but its combinatorial search spaces can become impractical. The Latent Program Network moves this search into a learned, compact space of implicit programs represented by neural input-output mappings.

LPN builds test-time search into its architecture. When presented with a new task, it uses gradients to search the latent program space. This avoids requiring a predefined domain-specific programming language while retaining an explicit adaptation process. The design combines neural representations with the ability to search for a task-appropriate transformation during use.

Across programming-by-examples tasks, LPN matches or exceeds the compared in-context learning and test-time training methods. On ARC-AGI, the authors demonstrate both learning a compact program space and searching it to adapt to novel tasks. Enabling test-time search doubles performance on the reported out-of-distribution tasks, indicating that the search process contributes substantially to adaptation beyond the learned representation alone.
neurips-2025-searching-latent-program-sp.tldr: Latent Program Networks adapt to new example-defined tasks by searching a learned program space with gradients at test time.

paragraphs: Understanding spatial relationships from visual input means inferring how objects are arranged and related in three dimensions. This ability matters for tasks such as navigation and embodied interaction. The paper identifies spatial uncertainty and limited training data as obstacles for pretrained vision-language models, then addresses both within a framework that preserves their existing architecture.

The first component, SpatialMind, structures the model's prompting process. It breaks complex scenes and questions into interpretable reasoning steps, giving spatial analysis a more explicit organization. The second component, ScanForgeQA, supplies question-answering data constructed automatically from diverse three-dimensional simulation scenes. This scalable dataset is designed for fine-tuning models on spatial understanding.

Experiments across multiple benchmarks demonstrate benefits from the prompting strategy and the fine-tuning strategy individually, as well as from their combination. The findings support improving spatial reasoning through both the way a question is approached and the examples used to train the model. Together, these components offer a route to enhancing pretrained models without redesigning their architecture.
neurips-2025-spatial-understanding-from-.tldr: Structured spatial prompts and automatically generated simulation questions improve pretrained vision-language models' spatial reasoning without architectural changes.

paragraphs: Spiking neural networks communicate through binary spikes, offering a route toward energy-efficient computation. Their performance gap has often been attributed to information loss from sparse, binary activations. This paper identifies a frequency bias: spiking neurons suppress high-frequency components while favoring low-frequency information. The authors argue that this imbalance explains degraded feature representations.

An experiment with Spiking Transformers supports the role of frequency handling: replacing average pooling with max pooling raises CIFAR-100 accuracy from 76.73% to 79.12%. The proposed Max-Former adds max pooling to patch embedding and replaces self-attention with depth-wise convolution. These changes are designed to strengthen high-frequency signals within the network.

Max-Former achieves 82.39% ImageNet top-1 accuracy with 63.99 million parameters, compared with Spikformer's 74.81% using 66.34 million. A related Max-ResNet-18 reaches 97.17% on CIFAR-10 and 83.06% on CIFAR-100. These results show that frequency-aware architectural changes can improve both Transformer-based and convolutional spiking models, supporting the paper's proposed explanation of their representation weaknesses.
neurips-2025-spiking-neural-networks-nee.tldr: The paper identifies high-frequency suppression in spiking neurons and improves tested spiking architectures with operators designed to restore that information.

paragraphs: Reinforcement learning can improve language-model reasoning, but lengthy answers may contain uncertain searches and repeated self-corrections. Thinker addresses this by restructuring question answering into separate stages that train quick judgment, checking, refinement, and concise explanation. The approach draws inspiration from the distinction between fast intuition and slower deliberation.

The model first answers under a strict token budget. It then evaluates that initial answer, revises it with more deliberation, and summarizes the refinement into precise steps. Each stage gives a different reasoning behavior an explicit role. In particular, the initial budget encourages an economical answer, while later stages create opportunities to inspect and improve it.

Average accuracy rises from 25.6% to 27.3% for Qwen2.5-1.5B and from 45.9% to 51.0% for DeepSeek-R1-Qwen-1.5B. Qwen's fast mode alone reaches 25.2% using fewer than 1,000 tokens. These findings suggest that quick judgment and deliberative reasoning can benefit from targeted training as complementary capabilities, with the fast mode offering a useful efficiency result in the reported evaluation.
neurips-2025-thinker-learning-to-think-f.tldr: Thinker trains fast answering, verification, deliberate refinement, and summarization as separate stages, improving reported accuracy while enabling efficient short answers.

paragraphs: Video generators can produce objects that change shape implausibly as they move. This paper addresses that problem by giving a video model explicit information about three-dimensional geometry and motion. The approach augments ordinary two-dimensional videos with three-dimensional point trajectories aligned to the images, creating the PointVid dataset.

The authors use PointVid to fine-tune a latent diffusion model so it can track depicted objects using three-dimensional Cartesian coordinates. They then regularize object shape and motion to suppress unwanted artifacts, including nonphysical deformation. This connects the generated appearance to a representation of how the object's geometry moves through space.

The framework improves generated RGB video quality and reduces issues such as object morphing. It also handles contact-rich, task-oriented scenarios, where understanding the shapes and movements of interacting solids is important. The stated contribution is a way to improve visual plausibility through three-dimensional augmentation and regularization, with a design that can be integrated into existing video diffusion models.
neurips-2025-towards-physical-understand.tldr: Aligned 3D point trajectories and shape-and-motion regularization help video diffusion models reduce object morphing and generate more plausible interactions.

paragraphs: Retrieval-augmented generation combines information stored in model parameters with information supplied in context. This paper studies how those sources interact inside a language model, especially when they conflict. It treats information about entities as a flow through the network, allowing the authors to trace how entity-related content changes across layers.

A conventional trained linear probe cannot adapt to arbitrarily specified entities. The authors introduce an entity-aware probe that marks targets with special tokens and uses a small rank-8 LoRA update to process those markers. An attribution experiment verifies that the probe can detect information about newly specified entities within complex hidden representations.

The probing results indicate that contextual and parametric information travel between tokens through distinct attention-head sets, supporting competition within knowledge types. Conflicting information retains a residual presence across layers, while agreement between sources leads to accumulating information. The authors report that the magnitude of this accumulation determines its influence on final outputs. These observations provide an internal account of how mixed-source knowledge contributes to answers.
neurips-2025-understanding-parametric-an.tldr: Entity-aware probing traces distinct attention routes for stored and contextual knowledge and reveals how agreement accumulates to influence model outputs.

paragraphs: Identifying where ligands bind to proteins is an important step in structure-based drug design. The paper argues that organizing data around individual protein–ligand complexes overlooks binding sites observed in other complexes of the same protein. It also identifies problems with separating detection into segmentation and clustering, and with evaluation measures that inadequately reflect prediction quality.

UniSite-DS reorganizes the dataset around unique proteins. Compared with the previously most widely used datasets, it contains 4.81 times as much multi-site data and 2.08 times as much data overall. The UniSite model predicts binding sites end to end, using a set prediction loss with one-to-one matching to connect predicted sites with supervision.

The authors also introduce Average Precision based on intersection over union, measuring prediction quality through overlap. Experiments on UniSite-DS and other representative benchmarks support this metric as a more accurate reflection of prediction quality and show UniSite outperforming the compared state-of-the-art methods. The contribution links more complete protein-level data, unified prediction, and improved evaluation.
neurips-2025-unisite-the-first-cross-str.tldr: UniSite combines a protein-centric binding-site dataset, end-to-end set prediction, and overlap-based evaluation to improve ligand binding-site detection.
